Tennessee property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • A disputed assessment must generally first be appealed to the county board of equalization where the property is located or it becomes final. (Appealing to the State Board of Equalization (Value Appeals); source)
  • The county board of equalization generally convenes June 1 (Shelby County May 1). (Assessment Schedule (Tenn. Code Ann. 67-1-404); source)
  • Appeals to the State Board of Equalization from a county board must be filed by August 1 of the tax year or within 45 days of the date notice of the county board action was sent, whichever is later. (Appealing to the State Board of Equalization (Value Appeals); source)
  • An SBOE appeal is first heard by an Administrative Judge, who issues an Initial Decision and Order within 90 days of the hearing. (Value Appeals; source)
  • Judicial review of a final SBOE action requires a petition in chancery court within 60 days from when the order becomes final. (Value Appeals; source)
  • The appellant must show by a preponderance of the evidence the correct assessment; sales of comparable properties are generally the best evidence for residential property. (Value Appeals; source)
  • Taxpayers must pay at least the undisputed portion of taxes before the delinquency date to avoid penalties and interest while an appeal is pending. (Value Appeals (Tenn. Code Ann. 67-5-1512(b)); source)
  • Assessment ratios: residential real property 25%, farm real property 25%, commercial and industrial real property 40%, public utility property 55%, business personal property 30%. (Tennessee Property Assessment Glossary; source)
  • Within one year from the order confirming a delinquent tax sale, any person with a legal or equitable interest may redeem by paying the court clerk the taxes, interest, penalties, costs and court-ordered charges plus 10% per annum interest on the entire purchase price from the date of sale. (Tenn. Atty. Gen. Op. 12-085 (citing 67-5-2703, 67-5-2701(a), 67-5-2702(a)); source)
  • On the purchaser's motion the redeeming person may also have to pay property taxes and money the purchaser spent to preserve the property during redemption. (Tenn. Atty. Gen. Op. 12-085; source)

Tennessee offers property tax relief for qualifying homeowners, and official sources explain the rules.

What the official sources say

  • Tennessee's Property Tax Relief program reimburses part or all of paid property taxes for low-income elderly and disabled homeowners and disabled veteran homeowners or surviving spouses; it is not an exemption and the owner still receives and pays the tax bill. (Property Tax Relief (Comptroller); source)
  • Tax relief applies only to the primary residence, one property per tax year. (Property Tax Relief FAQ; source)
  • The program began in 1973 following the 1972 constitutional amendment. (Property Tax Relief (Comptroller); source)
  • A local-option property tax freeze for homeowners 65 or older exists in participating counties/cities; taxes on the principal residence are frozen at a base amount, subject to annual application and a county income limit. (Property Tax Freeze (Comptroller); source)
  • Tax Relief and Tax Freeze application deadlines are 35 days past the local property tax delinquency date. (Assessment Schedule (67-5-701(d)(1)); source)

title: Tennessee Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Tennessee Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Tennessee's inheritance tax is no longer imposed after December 31, 2015; do not file for decedents dying in 2016 or later. (Inheritance Tax (Dept. of Revenue); source)
Selling in Tennessee?
We buy Tennessee houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Is there still a Tennessee tax on what heirs receive?

No. Tennessee's inheritance tax is gone for anyone who died in 2016 or after. The Department of Revenue's page says the levy is no longer imposed after December 31, 2015, and it asks families not to file for those later deaths.

Back when it applied, the tax reached the portion of the net estate above an exemption tied to the year of death. Net estate meant the market value of every asset after subtracting items such as property passing to a surviving spouse, debts and administration costs, and the executor, administrator or trustee paid the bill from estate funds. A family listing an inherited house in Tennessee today skips that return entirely. The federal estate tax is the only one left, and it reaches very large estates.

At what size does the federal estate tax reach a Tennessee estate?

Only at a very high threshold. According to the IRS, the Working Families Tax Cuts law, Public Law 119-21 signed July 4, 2025, lifts the basic exclusion amount to $15,000,000 for 2026. Recent years looked like this.

Year of deathBasic exclusion amount
2023$12,920,000
2024$13,610,000
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

Source: IRS, What's new, estate and gift tax. The IRS notes the top bracket rate has stood at 40 percent since 2013. A typical Tennessee family house falls far under these numbers, so most estates never send a Form 706. Total the house with bank balances, retirement accounts and insurance owned at death before deciding no return is needed.

Can a widow or widower carry over the unused federal amount?

Yes. For decedents with a surviving spouse, an estate may elect, starting January 1, 2011, to pass the decedent's unused exclusion to that spouse. The election sits on a timely filed estate tax return, so a Form 706 can pay off even where no tax is owed.

The IRS adds that simplified valuation rules cover estates that would not need to file apart from the election. A surviving spouse in Tennessee who plans to sell the family home and hold a large portfolio should raise this with the estate's lawyer well ahead of the filing deadline.

Which value do heirs use when they sell an inherited Tennessee house?

They use the home's worth at the owner's death. IRS Publication 551 says inherited property generally takes its market value on that day, or on the alternate valuation date if the executor picked one. Suppose a house was worth $240,000 at death and sells for $245,000. The federal gain is $5,000, whatever the decedent paid decades earlier.

  • An estate that had to file a federal return gives each beneficiary a Schedule A (Form 8971) stating the estate tax value.
  • The IRS issued final regulations on September 16, 2024 for consistent basis reporting between an estate and a person acquiring property from it.
  • An estate under the filing requirement should skip Form 8971, since the IRS warns that sending it can produce needless letters.

For a smaller estate, hire a licensed appraiser to value the house as of the death and keep that report with the estate file.

What if a child gave the house to a parent shortly before the parent died?

The rule changes in this narrow case. Publication 551 carves out appreciated property that you or your spouse handed to the decedent during the final year of life; the death-day value does not govern it. When it comes back to you, your basis equals the decedent's adjusted basis immediately before death.

Appreciated property means an item whose market value on the day of the gift beat the giver's adjusted basis. Tennessee families who retitle a house to a relative and then inherit it back should talk with the estate's attorney first, so the tax effect is clear before anyone signs a deed.

Who owes the recording tax when the estate sells the house?

The buyer owes it, as the grantee. The Department of Revenue's recordation tax page says the county register of deeds gathers the tax, and its rate table sets realty transfer tax at $0.37 per $100 of purchase price. An estate sale at $180,000 therefore carries $666.

Property tax follows separate steps. The Comptroller's overview of assessment and taxation has the county assessor appraising the parcel, the county commission and city governing bodies fixing rates, and the county trustee and city officials collecting. Request the parcel's open balance from the trustee's office and pass it to the closing agent.

How will the county value the inherited house for property tax?

The assessor applies a 25 percent ratio to residential appraisals, so a $100,000 appraisal becomes a $25,000 assessment. Appraisals reset during reappraisal programs on a 6, 5 or 4 year cycle and generally hold steady between them unless buildings change.

  • An owner can challenge an overstated value, an understated value on someone else's parcel, or the way the parcel is classified.
  • Complaints about the dollar amount of the bill are not accepted as a reason.
  • The sequence runs from a conversation with the assessor to the county equalization board, which opens its sessions June 1, and on to the state board and Chancery Court.

An heir who receives an older house last appraised years ago may see a new number at the next reappraisal.

What papers should heirs gather before listing?

A tidy folder shortens closing and supports the basis you report later. Assemble these before the sign goes up.

  • A certified death certificate and the court order naming the person authorized to sign the deed.
  • The appraisal as of the death, or the Schedule A if a Form 706 was filed.
  • The newest tax bill, plus a payoff number from the trustee.
  • Receipts for additions the decedent paid for, because the IRS counts improvements that add value toward basis.
  • A payoff statement from any lender.

Give the title company copies early so the closer can tell whether the signer needs more authority than the folder shows. Missing court paperwork is a common reason an estate closing slips by days or weeks, so ask the clerk for certified copies in advance.

IRS Topic no. 409 mentions that a taxable gain can call for estimated tax payments, so ask the preparer about due dates once an offer is accepted.

Does an estate sale bring any other small tax item?

Two items can come up. The IRS fee for an estate tax closing letter, Letter 627, rose from $56 to $76 effective October 26, 2026, and it matters only to estates that filed a Form 706. The yearly gift exclusion is $19,000 per recipient for 2026, which can matter if a parent was moving the house to children before death.

On the court side, ask the clerk where the decedent lived which office handles letters of administration or probate of a will. That office can explain what the court must approve before a sale.

More questions about Tennessee Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Tennessee charge inheritance tax in 2026?

It does not. The Department of Revenue says the tax ended after December 31, 2015, and no return is due for deaths in 2016 or later.

What federal estate tax threshold applies this year?

For deaths in 2026 the basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000 per person, under Public Law 119-21. A surviving spouse can add the unused portion through an election on a timely filed return.

What starting value do heirs use for an inherited house?

Generally what the house was worth on the day the owner died. Any gain is measured from that figure.

Whose job is it to pay the deed tax on an estate sale?

The buyer pays $0.37 for each $100 of price when the deed is filed with the register.

Can heirs contest the county's value of an inherited house?

Yes, for a value set too high or a wrong classification. Talk to the assessor first, then take it to the county equalization board, which opens June 1.

title: Tennessee Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House
content:
Tennessee Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Cash Home Buyers in Tennessee
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Tennessee Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Tennessee Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House sale
  • Turn the Tennessee Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Tennessee House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Tennessee has no individual income tax on wages, employer-sponsored retirement income or most other forms of income. (HIT-18 (Dept. of Revenue Help Center); source)
Selling in Tennessee?
We buy Tennessee houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Will Tennessee take a share of my profit when I sell a house?

No. Tennessee collects nothing from a seller's profit at the state level. The Department of Revenue says its former Hall income tax reached only interest from bonds and notes and dividends from stock, and that levy ended for tax periods starting January 1, 2021 and later. The Department's help center separately states that wages, employer retirement income and most other forms of income carry no Tennessee individual income tax.

The tax question for a Tennessee seller is therefore a federal one. If a company or partnership holds title instead of a person, call the Department before you pick a closing date, since entity taxes are a different subject from the personal tax described here.

How much profit can a Tennessee homeowner shield from federal tax?

A single owner can shield the first $250,000 of profit on a main home, and spouses filing together can shield $500,000. IRS Topic no. 701 sets two requirements, ownership and use. Each must be satisfied for at least 24 months within the five years that end on the closing date, and the months need not overlap.

  • Spouses filing jointly need only one of them to pass the ownership test, but each must pass the use test personally.
  • An exclusion claimed on a different house in the preceding two years generally blocks a second one.
  • Members of the uniformed services, the Foreign Service and the intelligence community on qualified extended duty may elect to pause the five year clock for as long as ten years.

IRS Publication 523 supplies worksheets and the list of exceptions. Read it before assuming a sale in Knoxville, Memphis or a small Tennessee town creates no tax.

Do I still file anything if the whole profit is sheltered?

Sometimes. A Form 1099-S from the title company obliges you to report the sale even when none of the profit is taxable, according to the IRS. Reporting is also required if any slice of the profit sits above your limit.

The entry goes on Form 8949, which feeds Schedule D of Form 1040. Gather your closing statement from the original purchase, the settlement sheet from this sale and receipts for lasting improvements. Topic no. 703 defines basis as generally the cost of the asset, raised by improvements that add value and lowered by items such as depreciation and casualty reimbursements. A new roof or finished basement can trim the profit you report.

What federal rates hit profit beyond the shelter?

Profit on a house owned longer than a year is long-term. The IRS says most of it is taxed at no more than 15 percent for most individuals. The figures below come from IRS Topic no. 409 and describe taxable years beginning in 2025, so confirm the numbers for the year your Tennessee closing occurs.

Filing status0% rate through15% rate through
Single$48,350$533,400
Married filing jointly$96,700$600,050
Head of household$64,750$566,700
Married filing separately$48,350$300,000

Income above the 15 percent ceiling is taxed at 20 percent. A house sold within a year of purchase produces a short-term result, which is taxed like ordinary pay.

How does the calendar affect a Tennessee seller's result?

Topic no. 409 explains how the holding period is counted. You count from the day after you acquired the asset through the day you disposed of it, and more than one year makes the result long-term. A seller who closes on a Tennessee house two days short of the anniversary can move from the lower long-term brackets into ordinary income rates.

The same page raises two further points for owners who exceed the shelter. People with significant investment income may owe the net investment income tax, described in Topic no. 559, and a taxable gain can require estimated tax payments during the year of sale. It also states that a loss on a personal home is not deductible, so a sale below your cost brings no write off.

Do heirs who sell a Tennessee house owe tax on the whole price?

No, because heirs usually start from the home's worth at the owner's death rather than from the owner's old purchase price. Publication 551 says inherited property generally takes its market value on the day of death, or the value six months later when the executor selected the alternate valuation date. A sale near that figure leaves little profit to tax.

  • When the estate filed a federal return, each beneficiary generally gets a Schedule A (Form 8971) stating the value to use.
  • Without a Schedule A, Publication 551 allows the appraised value used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes.
  • Property you gave to someone who died within the next year, then received back, keeps the giver's basis.

Order an appraisal that names the date of death. It becomes your record on Schedule D.

What does Tennessee charge on the deed when the house changes hands?

The state levies a realty transfer tax through recordation. Its published rate is $0.37 per $100 of purchase price, which works out to $1,110 on a $300,000 sale. A county register collects the money and passes it along. The Department places the obligation on the grantee, the person taking title.

Lenders add a mortgage tax of $0.115 per $100 of debt after the first $2,000, and the borrower owes it. Phone your county's recording office to learn how it wants the purchase price shown on the deed.

How do payment plans and former rentals change the picture?

Seller financing spreads the profit across years. IRS Topic no. 705 treats any sale with a payment arriving after the year of closing as an installment sale, reported on Form 6252 unless you elect out. You count as income only the portion of each payment that exceeds your basis, while interest is ordinary income.

A house that served as a rental carries depreciation. Publication 551 fixes the depreciable basis at the smaller of the market value when rental use began or your adjusted basis then. Topic no. 409 adds that unrecaptured section 1250 gain on real property can be taxed at a top rate of 25 percent. A Tennessee landlord with a former home should ask a preparer for a projection before accepting an offer.

Which official pages hold the current figures?

Tax amounts shift each year, so confirm them at the source before you sign a contract.

  • IRS Topic no. 701 and Publication 523 for the main home exclusion.
  • IRS Topic no. 409 for rates and reporting forms.
  • IRS Publication 551 for inherited and gifted property.
  • Tennessee Department of Revenue pages for recordation tax and the Hall tax.

More questions about Tennessee Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Does Tennessee have a state tax on profit from selling a home?

Tennessee has no personal income tax on wages or most other income, and its Hall tax on interest and dividends stopped for periods beginning January 1, 2021. Federal rules still decide whether any profit is taxable.

How large is the profit shelter for a main home?

It is $250,000 for one owner and $500,000 on a joint return. You need 24 months of ownership plus 24 months of living there inside the five years before closing.

Will heirs be taxed on everything they get from a house sale?

Only on profit above the stepped-up starting value, generally the market value at death. Keep a dated appraisal on file with the estate papers.

What does Tennessee charge on a deed at closing?

The realty transfer tax runs $0.37 for every $100 of price, and the Department of Revenue says the person receiving the deed pays it.

Do I have to file a return for a sale with no taxable profit?

Only when you were sent a Form 1099-S or part of the profit exceeds your limit. In that case the sale goes on Form 8949 and Schedule D.
